lessons.title: Describe a place
lessons.sub: Use your senses to show a place
lessons.goal: I can describe a place with exact details from three senses and explain why it matters.
beats: say

Welcome to the board. I'm Ms. Bell. In this lesson, we are going to write about a topic together, from the first look at the prompt to the last period. I will write first, slowly, and say what I'm thinking. Then you write your own lines, and at the end you write a whole answer on the clock. The six steps we use will work on any topic you meet, on a test or in class.
head
Lesson 1 · Describe a place
Lesson 1. Describe a place.
write
Topic: Describe a place that is important to you. Tell what you see, hear, and feel there, and explain why it matters.

Here is the topic, just as it could appear on a test. Describe a place that is important to you. Tell what you see, hear, and feel there, and explain why it matters. Before I write one word, I read it twice.
write
① READ IT  **Describe** · a **place** · what you **see, hear, feel** · **why** it matters

Step one. Read it. I read the prompt twice and mark the task words. Describe is the job. Place is the topic. See, hear, and feel mean the prompt wants my senses. And why it matters means I must give a reason. Four marks. Four things my answer must do.
pick
Which one is NOT something this prompt asks you to do?
Describe a place
Use what you see, hear, and feel
Tell a story about a trip you took
The prompt asks for a place, your senses, and a reason. It does not ask for a story about a trip. Staying on the topic is the first thing a reader checks.
write
② BRAINSTORM IT  place: my grandmother's kitchen · see: yellow walls, big blue pot · smell: fresh tortillas · hear: radio, spoon on the pot · feel: warm, safe · why: my family comes together

Step two. Brainstorm it. I write notes fast, without full sentences. My place is my grandmother's kitchen. I see yellow walls and a big blue pot. I smell fresh tortillas. I hear the radio and a spoon on the pot. I feel warm and safe. And why it matters: my family comes together there. Messy notes are fine. Nobody grades the notes.
pick
Which note does NOT belong to the kitchen?
smell: fresh tortillas
sound: cars on the highway
feel: warm and safe
Cars on the highway do not belong in my grandmother's kitchen. When I brainstorm, I keep every note tied to my one place.
write
③ PLAN IT  1 Opening: place + why · 2 What I see and smell · 3 What I hear and feel · 4 Closing: why it matters

Step three. Plan it. Four parts: an opening with the place and the reason, one part for what I see and smell, one part for what I hear and feel, and a closing that returns to why it matters. A plan takes one minute and saves ten.
write
④ OPEN IT  My grandmother's kitchen is the place that matters most to me because it is where my family comes together.
Step four. Open it. My first sentence names the place and gives the reason, both at once. Now the reader knows exactly where we are going. I use words from the prompt: place, matters.
ask
Your turn. Write your opening: name your place and say why it matters. Type it in the notebook.
Your opening: name your place and say why it matters.
has_any
place
matters
important
because
Use words from the prompt: place, matters, important, because.
starts_upper
Start with a capital letter.
ends_punct
End with a period.
min_words
A full sentence, at least eight words.
The soccer field behind my house is the place that matters most to me because I feel free there.
That opening tells the reader the topic right away.
Look at the note under your line. A good opening names the topic in the first sentence.
say
Now the middle. This is where most of the points are earned, so I build it slowly.
write
⑤ When I walk in, I see yellow walls and a big blue pot on the stove. The smell of fresh tortillas fills the whole room.

Step five. Build it. The first body part: what I see and smell. Notice the exact words. Not a nice kitchen, but yellow walls and a big blue pot. Exact words make the reader see it. When I walk in, I see yellow walls and a big blue pot on the stove. The smell of fresh tortillas fills the whole room.
write
Then, I hear the radio playing old songs and my grandmother's spoon tapping the pot. Her voice is soft, and I feel warm and safe.

The second body part: what I hear and feel. Notice then, a small word that moves the reader along. Then, I hear the radio playing old songs and my grandmother's spoon tapping the pot. Her voice is soft, and I feel warm and safe.
ask
Your turn. Write one sentence about what you see or hear in your place. Use one exact detail, not a weak word like nice or good.
One sentence: what you see or hear. No nice, good, or thing.
has_any
see
saw
hear
smell
feel
look
Use a sense word: see, hear, smell, feel.
not_regex
\b(nice|good|thing|things)\b
Replace nice, good, or thing with an exact word.
starts_upper
Start with a capital letter.
min_words
At least seven words.
ends_punct
End with punctuation.
I see tall green grass and white lines, and I hear my friends shouting my name.
Yes. A reader can picture, or follow, that sentence.
Look at the note under your line and fix the first thing it names.
write
⑥ CLOSE IT  This kitchen matters because it makes me feel that I belong. No matter where I go, I will carry its smell and its warmth with me.

Step six. Close it. My last sentences return to why it matters, which is the question the prompt asked. A good closing says the answer one more time in new words, and then stops. This kitchen matters because it makes me feel that I belong. No matter where I go, I will carry its smell and its warmth with me.
pick
Now check it. Which sentence is correct?
i see a big blue pot on the stove
I see a big blue pot on the stove.
I seen a big blue pot on the stove.
The second one. It starts with a capital letter, it ends with a period, and it uses see, not seen. I check capitals, verbs, punctuation, and spelling, every time, after I write.
say

That is the routine: Read it. Brainstorm it. Plan it. Open it. Build it. Close it and check it. Six steps, in that order, every time. Now you do the whole thing, on the clock. I will give you the same topic, or you can choose another from the list.
clear
Board wiped. Your turn.
task
Your topic. Describe a place that is important to you. Tell what you see, hear, and feel there, and explain why it matters. Read it, brainstorm, plan in the five boxes, then write. Go.
Topic: Describe a place that is important to you. Tell what you see, hear, and feel there, and explain why it matters.
My first sentence names a place and says why it matters.
I used at least three senses or exact details: see, hear, smell, feel.
I used exact words instead of nice, good, or thing.
Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.
My last sentences return to why the place matters.

The place that matters most to me is my grandmother's kitchen because it is where my family comes together. When I walk in, I see yellow walls and a big blue pot on the stove. The smell of fresh tortillas fills the whole room. Then, I hear the radio playing old songs and my grandmother's spoon tapping the pot. Her voice is soft, and I feel warm and safe. This kitchen matters because it makes me feel that I belong. No matter where I go, I will carry its smell and its warmth with me.

Here is a five. The place that matters most to me is my grandmother's kitchen because it is where my family comes together. When I walk in, I see yellow walls and a big blue pot on the stove. The smell of fresh tortillas fills the whole room. Then, I hear the radio playing old songs and my grandmother's spoon tapping the pot. Her voice is soft, and I feel warm and safe. This kitchen matters because it makes me feel that I belong. No matter where I go, I will carry its smell and its warmth with me. Why is it a five? The first sentence names the place and the reason. It uses three senses with exact details. It never says nice or good. And the last sentences answer the question the prompt asked, why it matters.
Place + why
What I see
What I hear
How I feel
Closing
say
You just described a place with the six steps. Next lesson, a different kind of topic: explaining how to do something. The routine stays the same.

lessons.title: Explain how to do something
lessons.sub: Clear steps for a new person
lessons.goal: I can explain a process in clear steps with First, Next, Then, Finally for a reader who is new to it.
beats: say

Welcome back. This is a different kind of topic: explaining how to do something. But the routine is the same six steps, and you will see that the steps work again. This time the secret is the reader. Your reader has never done this before, so every step has to be clear.
head
Lesson 2 · Explain how to do something
Lesson 2. Explain how to do something.
write
Topic: Choose something you know how to do. Explain how to do it, step by step, so a new person could do it too.

Here is the topic, just as it could appear on a test. Choose something you know how to do. Explain how to do it, step by step, so a new person could do it too. Before I write one word, I read it twice.
write
① READ IT  **Explain how** · something you **know** · **step by step** · for a **new person**
Step one. Read it. Explain how is the job. Something you know is the topic, and I choose it. Step by step tells me the shape: steps, in order. And a new person is my reader. Four marks.
pick
Who is your reader?
Someone who already knows how to do it
A new person who has never done it
Only your best friend
A new person. That means no skipped steps. If I forget to say crack the egg, a new person is lost.
write
② BRAINSTORM IT  topic: how to make scrambled eggs · need: eggs, pan, fork, butter, salt · steps: crack, beat, melt butter, pour, stir, serve · careful: the pan is hot

Step two. Brainstorm it. My topic is scrambled eggs. First, what you need: eggs, a pan, a fork, butter, salt. Then the steps in order: crack, beat, melt the butter, pour, stir, serve. And one warning: the pan is hot.
pick
Which note does NOT belong in how to make scrambled eggs?
steps: crack, beat, stir
need: eggs, pan, butter
my favorite soccer team
My favorite soccer team. It is a fine thing to know, but it does not help a new person make eggs. In a how-to, every note helps the reader do the job.
write
③ PLAN IT  1 Opening: what + why it is easy · 2 What you need · 3 Steps: First, Next, Then · 4 A warning or tip · 5 Closing

Step three. Plan it. An opening that says what and why it is easy. What you need. The steps with First, Next, Then. A warning. And a closing. Notice that the steps are the biggest part, because the steps are what the reader came for.
write
④ OPEN IT  Scrambled eggs are easy to make, and anyone can learn how in five minutes.
Step four. Open it. One sentence that says what I will teach, and gives the reader a reason to keep reading: it is easy, and it takes five minutes.
ask
Your turn. Write your opening: say what you will teach and one reason it is easy or useful.
Your opening: what you will teach, and why it is easy or useful.
has_any
how to
easy
learn
simple
useful
can
will
Say what you will teach: how to, easy, learn, simple, useful.
starts_upper
Start with a capital letter.
ends_punct
End with a period.
min_words
A full sentence, at least eight words.
Making a paper airplane is simple, and you only need one sheet of paper.
That opening tells the reader the topic right away.
Look at the note under your line. A good opening names the topic in the first sentence.
say
Now the middle. This is where most of the points are earned, so I build it slowly.
write
⑤ First, gather what you need: two eggs, a pan, a fork, a little butter, and a pinch of salt.

Step five. Build it. The first body part: what you need. First, with a comma, tells the reader this is the start. First, gather what you need: two eggs, a pan, a fork, a little butter, and a pinch of salt.
write
Next, crack the eggs into a bowl and beat them with the fork. Then, melt the butter in the pan on low heat. After that, pour in the eggs and stir slowly until they are soft and yellow.

The steps. Watch the signal words: Next, Then, After that. Each one has a comma. And each step starts with a command verb: crack, beat, melt, pour, stir. Next, crack the eggs into a bowl and beat them with the fork. Then, melt the butter in the pan on low heat. After that, pour in the eggs and stir slowly until they are soft and yellow.
write
Be careful: the pan is hot, so never touch it without a towel.
And the warning. A good teacher thinks about what could go wrong. Be careful: the pan is hot, so never touch it without a towel.
ask
Your turn. Write one step. Start with First, Next, Then, or Finally, add a comma, and use a command verb like crack, stir, or fold.
One step: a signal word, a comma, and a command verb.
has_regex
^(First|Next|Then|After that|Finally),
Start with First, Next, Then, After that, or Finally, and put a comma after it.
min_words
At least six words.
ends_punct
End with punctuation.
Next, fold the paper in half so the edges match.
Yes. A reader can picture, or follow, that sentence.
Look at the note under your line and fix the first thing it names.
write
⑥ CLOSE IT  Finally, put the eggs on a plate and enjoy them while they are warm. Now you know how to make breakfast for yourself.

Step six. Close it. A how-to ends with the finish line: the last step and the result. Finally, put the eggs on a plate and enjoy them while they are warm. Now you know how to make breakfast for yourself.
pick
Now check it. Which step is written best for a new person?
Then you stir the eggs it is easy.
Then, stir the eggs slowly until they are soft.
Then stirring eggs slow.
The second one. It has a signal word and a comma, a command verb, and it tells how: slowly, and until what. The first one runs two ideas together. The third one has no real verb.
say

That is the routine: Read it. Brainstorm it. Plan it. Open it. Build it. Close it and check it. Six steps, in that order, every time. Now you do the whole thing, on the clock. I will give you the same topic, or you can choose another from the list.
clear
Board wiped. Your turn.
task
Your topic. Choose something you know how to do. Explain how to do it, step by step, so a new person could do it too. Read it, brainstorm, plan in the five boxes, then write. Go.
Topic: Choose something you know how to do. Explain how to do it, step by step, so a new person could do it too.
My first sentence says what I will teach.
I listed what the reader needs.
My steps are in order, with First, Next, Then, Finally and a comma after each.
Each step starts with a command verb.
I gave one warning or tip, and a closing.

Scrambled eggs are easy to make, and anyone can learn how in five minutes. First, gather what you need: two eggs, a pan, a fork, a little butter, and a pinch of salt. Next, crack the eggs into a bowl and beat them with the fork. Then, melt the butter in the pan on low heat. After that, pour in the eggs and stir slowly until they are soft and yellow. Be careful: the pan is hot, so never touch it without a towel. Finally, put the eggs on a plate and enjoy them while they are warm. Now you know how to make breakfast for yourself.

Here is a five. Scrambled eggs are easy to make, and anyone can learn how in five minutes. First, gather what you need: two eggs, a pan, a fork, a little butter, and a pinch of salt. Next, crack the eggs into a bowl and beat them with the fork. Then, melt the butter in the pan on low heat. After that, pour in the eggs and stir slowly until they are soft and yellow. Be careful: the pan is hot, so never touch it without a towel. Finally, put the eggs on a plate and enjoy them while they are warm. Now you know how to make breakfast for yourself. Why is it a five? The first sentence says what and why it is easy. The things needed come before the steps. The steps are in order with signal words and commas, and each one starts with a command verb. There is a warning, and a closing.
What + why easy
What you need
Steps
Warning / tip
Closing
say
You just explained a process with the six steps. Next lesson: telling about a time. That one needs the past tense.

lessons.title: Tell about a time
lessons.sub: A short story in the past tense
lessons.goal: I can tell a short true story with a beginning, a middle, and an end, in the past tense, and say what I learned.
beats: say

Welcome back. Today's topic asks for a story: a time that really happened to you. A story has its own shape, and it has its own grammar trap, the past tense. We will use the same six steps, and I will show you where the past tense matters.
head
Lesson 3 · Tell about a time
Lesson 3. Tell about a time.
write
Topic: Write about a time you learned something important. Tell what happened and what you learned.
Here is the topic, just as it could appear on a test. Write about a time you learned something important. Tell what happened and what you learned. Before I write one word, I read it twice.
write
① READ IT  **Write about** · a **time** · what **happened** · what you **learned**

Step one. Read it. Write about a time. A time is something that already happened, so I will write in the past. What happened is the story. What you learned is the lesson, and the prompt asks for it, so I must not forget it.
pick
Which verb form will most of your sentences use?
I learn
I learned
I will learn
I learned. A time that already happened is told in the past: learned, walked, felt, said. If the verbs are in the past, the reader hears a story.
write
② BRAINSTORM IT  time: my first day at a new school · beginning: scared, no friends · middle: a boy shared his lunch · end: I learned to say hello first

Step two. Brainstorm it. My time is my first day at a new school. Beginning: I was scared and had no friends. Middle: a boy sat with me and shared his lunch. End: I learned that I can say hello first.
pick
Which note is the MIDDLE of the story, the thing that happened?
beginning: scared, no friends
middle: a boy shared his lunch
end: I learned to say hello first
A boy shared his lunch. The beginning sets up the problem, the middle is what happens, and the end is what I learned.
write
③ PLAN IT  1 Opening: when + what I learned · 2 Beginning: the problem · 3 Middle: what happened (Then, Suddenly) · 4 End: what I learned
Step three. Plan it. An opening that says when it happened. A beginning with the problem. A middle with what happened, using Then and Suddenly. And an end with what I learned.
write
④ OPEN IT  Last September, on my first day at a new school, I learned that one small hello can change everything.
Step four. Open it. I begin with when it happened: last September. Then I hint at what I learned. A reader who sees a time word and a hint wants to read on.
ask
Your turn. Write your opening: say when it happened and hint at what you learned.
Your opening: when it happened + a hint of what you learned.
has_regex
\b(last|ago|year|day|week|month|once|when|summer|winter|spring|fall|september|october|november|december|january|february|march|april|may|june|july|august|morning|night)\b
Say when it happened: last year, two years ago, one day.
starts_upper
Start with a capital letter.
ends_punct
End with a period.
min_words
A full sentence, at least eight words.
Two years ago, when I moved to a new country, I learned that being brave is a choice.
That opening tells the reader the topic right away.
Look at the note under your line. A good opening names the topic in the first sentence.
say
Now the middle. This is where most of the points are earned, so I build it slowly.
write
⑤ At first, I was scared. I walked into the cafeteria and could not find one person I knew. My hands were shaking, and I sat alone.

Step five. Build it. The beginning, the problem. Listen to the verbs: was, walked, could not find, shaking, sat. All past. At first, I was scared. I walked into the cafeteria and could not find one person I knew. My hands were shaking, and I sat alone.
write
Then, a boy with a red backpack sat down next to me and shared his lunch. He smiled and said, "Hi, I am Marcos." Suddenly, my fear felt smaller.

The middle, what happened. Then and Suddenly move the story forward. And notice the exact details: a red backpack, a smile, his name. Then, a boy with a red backpack sat down next to me and shared his lunch. He smiled and said, Hi, I am Marcos. Suddenly, my fear felt smaller.
ask
Your turn. Write one sentence about what happened. Use a time word like then or suddenly and a past-tense verb like walked, saw, felt, or said.
One sentence: a time word + a past-tense verb.
has_any
then
suddenly
after that
next
finally
first
later
at first
Use a time word: then, suddenly, after that, later.
has_regex
\b\w+ed\b|\b(was|were|saw|felt|said|went|came|took|gave|made|ran|sat|began|knew|told|found|got|had)\b
Use a past-tense verb: walked, saw, felt, said, went.
min_words
At least seven words.
ends_punct
End with punctuation.
Then, I opened my notebook and said hello to the girl next to me.
Yes. A reader can picture, or follow, that sentence.
Look at the note under your line and fix the first thing it names.
write
⑥ CLOSE IT  That day I learned that I do not have to wait for friendship; I can start it. Now, when a new student arrives, I am the first to say hello.

Step six. Close it. The prompt asked what I learned, so my ending says it directly. That day I learned that I do not have to wait for friendship; I can start it. Now, when a new student arrives, I am the first to say hello. See how the last line shows the lesson in action.
pick
Now check it. Which sentence keeps the story in the past?
Then, he sits next to me and shared his lunch.
Then, he sat next to me and shared his lunch.
Then, he sit next to me and share his lunch.
The second one. Sat and shared are both past. The first one jumps from sits to shared. When I check, I read only the verbs, and I ask: is every one the same time?
say

That is the routine: Read it. Brainstorm it. Plan it. Open it. Build it. Close it and check it. Six steps, in that order, every time. Now you do the whole thing, on the clock. I will give you the same topic, or you can choose another from the list.
clear
Board wiped. Your turn.
task
Your topic. Write about a time you learned something important. Tell what happened and what you learned. Read it, brainstorm, plan in the five boxes, then write. Go.
Topic: Write about a time you learned something important. Tell what happened and what you learned.
My first sentence says when it happened.
My story has a beginning, a middle, and an end.
Most verbs are in the past tense, and I checked each one.
I used time words: at first, then, suddenly, after that.
I said clearly what I learned.

Last September, on my first day at a new school, I learned that one small hello can change everything. At first, I was scared. I walked into the cafeteria and could not find one person I knew. My hands were shaking, and I sat alone. Then, a boy with a red backpack sat down next to me and shared his lunch. He smiled and said, "Hi, I am Marcos." Suddenly, my fear felt smaller. That day I learned that I do not have to wait for friendship; I can start it. Now, when a new student arrives, I am the first to say hello.

Here is a five. Last September, on my first day at a new school, I learned that one small hello can change everything. At first, I was scared. I walked into the cafeteria and could not find one person I knew. My hands were shaking, and I sat alone. Then, a boy with a red backpack sat down next to me and shared his lunch. He smiled and said, "Hi, I am Marcos." Suddenly, my fear felt smaller. That day I learned that I do not have to wait for friendship; I can start it. Now, when a new student arrives, I am the first to say hello. Why is it a five? The first sentence tells when. There is a clear beginning, middle, and end. The verbs stay in the past. Time words move the story along, and the ending says directly what was learned.
When + hint
Beginning
Middle
End
What I learned
say
That was a story with the six steps. Next lesson: an opinion, where you must give reasons and examples.

lessons.title: Give your opinion
lessons.sub: A claim, two reasons, and the other side
lessons.goal: I can state an opinion that answers the question and support it with two reasons, examples, and a nod to the other side.
beats: say

Welcome back. Now the topic that appears most often: an opinion question. Should students do this, should schools do that. The six steps stay the same. What changes is the shape of the middle: reasons, and an example for each reason.
head
Lesson 4 · Give your opinion
Lesson 4. Give your opinion.
write
Topic: Should students have homework on weekends? Explain your opinion with reasons and examples.
Here is the topic, just as it could appear on a test. Should students have homework on weekends? Explain your opinion with reasons and examples. Before I write one word, I read it twice.
write
① READ IT  **Should** students have homework on weekends? · my **opinion** · **reasons** · **examples**
Step one. Read it. Should is the signal for an opinion: yes or no. Explain with reasons and examples tells me what to build. So my answer needs a claim, reasons, and an example for each one.
pick
What does the word should ask you for?
A story about your weekend
Your opinion: yes or no, and why
A list of weekend games
Your opinion, yes or no, and why. A should question is never answered with a story. It is answered with a claim and reasons.
write

② BRAINSTORM IT  opinion: NO homework on weekends · reason 1: students need rest (example: tired on Monday) · reason 2: family time (example: cooking together) · other side: practice helps, but 20 minutes is enough

Step two. Brainstorm it. My opinion: no homework on weekends. Reason one: students need rest. My example: I come to class tired on Monday. Reason two: family time. My example: my family cooks together on Sunday. And the other side: some teachers say practice helps, and that is fair, so twenty minutes is enough.
pick
Which note is the example for the reason rest?
I come to Monday class tired when I work all weekend.
Some teachers give long projects.
Families eat dinner together.
I come to Monday class tired. It is a real situation that shows the reason. An example is a small picture of the reason.
write
③ PLAN IT  1 Opening: my claim · 2 Reason 1 + example · 3 Reason 2 + example · 4 The other side · 5 Closing
Step three. Plan it. The claim. Reason one with its example. Reason two with its example. A sentence about the other side. And a closing. Five parts, five boxes.
write
④ OPEN IT  In my opinion, students should not have homework on weekends.
Step four. Open it. One sentence that answers the question with the words of the prompt: students, homework, weekends. The reader knows my side right away.
ask
Your turn. Write your claim: yes or no, in one sentence that uses the words homework and weekends.
Your claim: yes or no, with homework and weekends.
has_any
homework
Use the word homework from the prompt.
has_any
weekend
Use the word weekends from the prompt.
has_any
should
opinion
think
believe
Give an opinion: should, I think, I believe, in my opinion.
starts_upper
Start with a capital letter.
ends_punct
End with a period.
min_words
A full sentence, at least eight words.
I believe students should have a little homework on weekends.
That opening tells the reader the topic right away.
Look at the note under your line. A good opening names the topic in the first sentence.
say
Now the middle. This is where most of the points are earned, so I build it slowly.
write
⑤ First, students need rest. For example, when I work all weekend, I come to class tired on Monday and cannot focus.

Step five. Build it. Reason one, with First and a comma, and then For example. The example is a real situation, not a general idea. First, students need rest. For example, when I work all weekend, I come to class tired on Monday and cannot focus.
write
Second, weekends are for family. As a result, students who spend Saturday with their families feel happier and ready to learn.

Reason two. Second, with a comma. And As a result shows what the reason causes. Second, weekends are for family. As a result, students who spend Saturday with their families feel happier and ready to learn.
write
However, some teachers say practice helps, and that is true. A short reading assignment of twenty minutes is enough.

And the other side. However tells the reader I heard the other opinion. I agree with a part of it, and still hold my claim. However, some teachers say practice helps, and that is true. A short reading assignment of twenty minutes is enough.
ask
Your turn. Write one reason. Start with First or Second and a comma, then add an example that starts with For example.
One reason + an example: First or Second, then For example.
has_regex
^(First|Second|Also|In addition|Another reason)
Start with First, Second, Also, or In addition.
has_any
for example
for instance
such as
Add an example: For example, For instance, such as.
min_words
At least twelve words, a reason and an example.
ends_punct
End with punctuation.
Second, weekends are for family. For example, my family cooks together on Sunday.
Yes. A reader can picture, or follow, that sentence.
Look at the note under your line and fix the first thing it names.
write
⑥ CLOSE IT  In conclusion, students need weekends to rest and to be with their families. Short, smart assignments during the week are better for everyone.

Step six. Close it. In conclusion, with a comma, and then the claim again in new words. In conclusion, students need weekends to rest and to be with their families. Short, smart assignments during the week are better for everyone.
pick

① READ IT: the first word is the job
**Describe** → senses and exact details
**Explain how** → steps in order
**Tell about a time** → past tense: beginning, middle, end
**Should / opinion** → claim + two reasons + examples
**Compare** → alike and different

Step one is always the same: find the job word. Describe means senses and exact details. Explain how means steps in order. Tell about a time means past tense, with a beginning, a middle, and an end. Should or opinion means a claim, two reasons, and examples. And compare means how things are alike and how they are different. The job word tells you the shape of your answer.

The person who helps me most is my grandfather because he teaches me patience. First, he teaches me guitar. For example, every Sunday he sits with me for an hour and shows me one new chord.
